### [RankCast: Phase-Aware Rank Balancing in MoE Serving](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.33542>)

RankCast balances expert-parallel MoE serving against different bottlenecks: peak token load during prefill and peak active-expert count during decode. It overlaps next-layer routing prediction and compact load metadata with existing DeepEP communication, then adjusts rank prices or closes selected experts to reduce stragglers. On two Qwen deployments using H800 GPUs, prefill input throughput improves by up to 19.4% and median decode time per output token falls, with measured quality changes below one percentage point rather than lossless routing.

**Public availability:** 2026-11-26T01:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Paper](<https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.33542v1>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Read the scientific main text, pages 1–10, and all scientific Appendices A–D on pages 14–23 of the 23-page manuscript. Source pages 8, 9 and 20 were directly viewed. Prefill uses a protected true top-2 prefix and one histogram-based dual sweep with load feedback; decode greedily closes experts using predicted candidate sets. Metadata piggybacks on DeepEP dispatch and the solvers overlap model work. BF16 Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507 has separate eight-H800 prefill and decode nodes, TP8/EP8 each. Qwen3.5-397B-A17B uses both phases across sixteen H800s on two nodes, with DP16 attention and EP16. Software is SGLang 0.5.12, DeepEP 1.2.1 and DeepGEMM. Against native Top-k on the same deployment, Table 1 reports 4.2–19.4% higher prefill input throughput; the maximum is the 235B ShareGPT case at 8K tokens per rank. Table 3 gives median decode TPOT of 27.41→25.33 ms on 235B CodeContests and 52.19→46.97 ms on 397B CodeContests, with 1,024 forced output tokens and 96/128 in-flight requests. Its gain column measures reciprocal TPOT, not percent latency reduction. Eight-benchmark main settings have at most a 0.84 percentage-point quality loss; Appendix Table 8 gives a largest recorded loss of 0.85 points. The original November 26 DC batch and official schedule infer announcement on November 26 at 01:00 UTC. The earlier matching Recipe LG catalog completion is preserved. No author code release was verified.

**Limitations:** Rerouting is lossy. Prefill retains the target router’s true protected prefix, whereas decode protects predictions: true top-2 retention is 87.9–97.8%, not guaranteed. The single prefill sweep and greedy closure search do not prove a global optimum. Only two models from one family and at most sixteen physical GPUs are evaluated; larger-EP results are offline captured-score replays. Qwen3.5 TPOT excludes interleaved prefill chunks, and full serving throughput may bottleneck elsewhere. Many LongBench, EPLB and decode cells are single-run; natural-length 235B decode averages two runs, and prefill generally uses two or three. Quality sample sizes and repeat counts differ; some changes are statistically significant. Placement plus rerouting was not evaluated. No independent reproduction or author-code execution is claimed.

## [2026-11-26](../../../reports/2026/11/2026-11-26.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [PipeAxes: Decoupling Compute and Communication Granularities for Pipeline-Parallel LLM Serving](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34615>)

PipeAxes uses wide prefill batches but yields between layer slices, allowing decode requests to run without repeatedly loading every layer’s weights for small token chunks. It separately sizes compressed activation row groups and prioritizes short transfers, giving the scheduler independent control over GPU occupancy and network blocking. Physical-GPU replays with shaped Ethernet links show 1.17–2.16× the goodput of a calibrated Revisit-PP port in the tested two-stage WAN sweep; the gains depend on workload, latency targets and lossy INT4 transport.

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Read all scientific text on pages 1–10 through Availability in the 13-page manuscript; the remaining text is references, with no scientific appendix. Source pages 7 and 9 were directly viewed. LayerSpool retains batch/KV metadata and intermediate tensors, resumes prefill at layer boundaries, isolates decode CUDA graphs and gates decode on consumed-row watermarks. A Hadamard-INT4 codec merges hidden and residual tensors; independently sized activation row groups travel on striped TCP with express-frame priority. Affine startup calibration and online recursive least squares guide batch width, slice depth and transport groups. Experiments use BF16 Qwen3-8B, 30B-A3B and 32B, two 80 GB PCIe A800s without NVLink/P2P, and two 24 GB RTX 4090s plus two 24 GB RTX 3090s over 1 GbE. Linux netem shapes 100–1,000 Mbps and 30 ms RTT, with optional jitter/loss. Baselines share vLLM 0.23.0 V2 and kernels; Revisit-PP is the authors’ calibrated port and uses the same compressed priority transport on WAN. Across 97 paired replays and 5,016 requests, goodput requires all TTFT, TPOT and per-request p95 inter-token targets; target values and coding-agent multipliers depend on workload. The two-stage 8B/250 Mbps sweep reports 1.17–2.16× Revisit-PP goodput and 1.30–2.33× the best static grid. One bandwidth-swing run meets 74/74 targets versus 46/74; a separate four-stage MoE stress replay meets 16/21 versus 1/21, yielding 23.3× goodput from unrounded rates. The mixed 64K 32B case meets all fifteen short-request targets, but eight long requests miss the 12-second TTFT objective because computation alone exceeds fourteen seconds. INT4 quality is tested on Qwen3-8B: MMLU 75.02→75.08%, GSM8K 90.30→89.84%, and a 24-prompt SCBench subset 15→16 correct. The original November 26 DC batch and official schedule infer announcement on November 26 at 01:00 UTC. The paper promises future code and replay logs; no author release was verified.

**Limitations:** These are shaped-link experiments on physical GPUs, not measurements of a geographically deployed WAN. Large goodput ratios can have only 9, 21 or 23 requests and very small baseline denominators. Individual tail latencies still miss targets under overload; the 74-request success does not establish a universal SLO guarantee. Prefix caching is disabled and only selected Qwen models/topologies are implemented. INT4 transport is lossy; quality evaluation covers one 8B model with limited uncertainty reporting and only 24 long-context retrieval prompts. Fixed-512 can complete coding sessions faster while violating token-latency objectives. Agent replays use extracted lengths/timing and prescribed turn spacing, rather than closed-loop coding success. Code and raw logs are promised rather than verified; no independent experiments were run.

## [2026-11-21](../../../reports/2026/11/2026-11-21.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [Aggron: Aggressive Compression of Agentic KV Caches during Head-of-Line Stalls in the Request Queue](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26435>)

Aggron compresses an agent’s prose tail while its request waits for KV-memory admission, retaining the latest protected tool-output prefix and using a separate summary queue plus a latency predictor to hide compaction behind existing stalls. In trace-driven Qwen3.6-35B-A3B simulations at high offered load, it improves throughput by 1.34–1.40× and reduces program p99 latency by 27–31% against Slipstream and APEC, suggesting a practical way to turn admission delays into memory savings. Those system gains are simulated rather than measured under concurrent live Aggron traffic; separate live compression-arm quality checks have wide noise bands and do not prove adaptive-controller quality equivalence, while low-memory-pressure configurations can regress.

## [2026-11-19](../../../reports/2026/11/2026-11-19.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [Harvesting Expert-Parallel Bubbles for Fine-Tuning](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24496>)

BubbleTea predicts each GPU’s idle window inside an expert-parallel MoE layer and fills it with compiler-generated LoRA training chunks that share serving weights. On four A100 GPUs with BF16 serving across three MoE models, it delivers 1.9–6.2× the fine-tuning throughput of a ported LLMStation baseline while keeping both p90 TTFT and TPOT within 10% of serving alone in 50 of 63 workloads. It offers a concrete way to reclaim serving capacity, but those gains include improved decode/idle-time execution; residual bubble filling adds 12–23% at high load with expert load balancing, and some configurations substantially worsen serving latency.

## [2026-11-19](../../../reports/2026/11/2026-11-19.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [Cap-and-Track: Optimizing LLM Inference Request Dispatch Across Shifting Capacity](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24891>)

Cap-and-Track keeps excess asynchronous inference work in durable priority queues, combines prompt per-replica refusals with a refusal-driven dispatcher, and follows capacity changes without predicting output length. In a same-traffic production A/B, Meta’s complete shaper served a classifier on 39 H100s versus 68 for its fixed-rate precursor with matching coverage and scores; controlled real-engine replay separately tests admission and dispatch. The design is useful for latency-tolerant backfills and media processing, but the smaller fleet trades lower-priority freshness for utilization: the lowest band waited a median 6.6 hours versus 0.5 hours at backfill peaks, and interactive or agent-session traffic was not evaluated.

### [Superfluid: New Local and Heterogeneous-Fleet Evaluation of an Existing LLM Server](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17753>)

A new study of the existing Superfluid server evaluates priority scheduling, cached-prefix reuse and whole-session placement across local machines that each hold a complete model replica. In a six-device heterogeneous fleet, all 5,041 requests complete as nodes join and one is killed, while output throughput rises from 112 to 534 tokens per second. It provides a practical reference for resilient local agent serving, although fleet placement lacks a controlled baseline and model sharding is unsupported.

### [Cairn: Sharing and Prewarming Serverless LLM Startup Work](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16180>)

Cairn separates LLM startup into reusable model artifacts, model-independent setup that can run early, and process-bound CUDA graph capture, sharing the first group and replenishing prepared workers from a template process. On two emulated servers with RTX A6000 GPUs, this cuts cold starts by 4.1–5.2× for the tested 1B–14B models, offering a way to reduce serverless waiting beyond faster weight loading.

### [Reducing Batch Makespan through Inference–Environment Coordination](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16661>)

This system jointly chooses hybrid-model cache allocation, trajectory-aware inference routing and scheduling, and separate limits for admitted tasks and executing environment jobs. Advancing long action chains helps finish batches sooner: the combined design reduces measured makespan by 10.4–65.0% across the tested Ling agent workloads, while the added chain scheduler contributes a smaller 3.1–8.5% on live MCP-Atlas runs.

### [AFORE: Attention-FFN Disaggregation with Overlapped Reconfiguration of Experts](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03203>)

AFORE uses the upcoming microbatch's actual expert-routing demand to rebalance expert replicas in serving systems that separate attention from feed-forward computation. By copying expert weights while earlier microbatches run and accounting for exposed migration cost, it reduces expert bottlenecks without placing every reconfiguration on the request's critical path.

**Published:** 2026-10-02 · **First seen:** 2026-10-05T10:03:36Z · **Novelty:** newly-discovered · **Tags:** MoE Serving, Attention-FFN Disaggregation, Expert Placement

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Original v1 was submitted October 2 at 12:20:29 UTC; the October 5 announcement list and official schedule place public release at October 5 00:00 UTC, inside the main window. The older submission date is retained with the legacy newly-discovered label. Sections 7.1–7.2 test GLM-4.5-Air on 16 A100 GPUs across four dynamic workloads, reporting 10.1–17.6% higher output throughput and 7.1–9.5% lower P95 inter-token latency than the strongest competing baseline for each workload.

**Limitations:** Evaluation uses one model and two nodes. Expert replicas require spare memory, and successful overlap depends on pipeline timing and interconnect bandwidth; the observed hidden migrations are not a general guarantee. Vosti combines a formally verified inference engine with checked GPU-kernel contracts so batching, prompt chunking, and cache reuse preserve identical output logits under a fixed deployment configuration. SpecScale prunes uncompetitive reasoning branches early, shares computation between identical prefixes, and batches process-reward verification across requests. ### [SPLASH: Switching Parallel Layouts of Attention with Seamless Handoff for LLM Serving](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37626>)

SPLASH changes attention parallelism while requests are running by reusing resident weights and KV caches, transferring missing state in the background, and switching at a batch boundary. This lets serving systems adapt to changing concurrency and context lengths; its additional ownership layout stores attention weights and each request's cache without replicating either.

### [Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180>)

PagedAttention stores key-value caches in dynamically allocated blocks, allowing vLLM to avoid large contiguous reservations and share cached state across related sequences. More efficient memory use permits larger concurrent batches, making this a foundational open reference for high-throughput language-model serving.
